messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Mereana Taito is a 66-year-old American woman of Pacific Islander background who came to treatment after years of trying to live around memories she still could not fully tell. Divorced and living alone, she works as a curriculum designer, a job she has kept partly because much of it can be done from home. When she first spoke about the event, she did not begin with a smooth account. She would stop, go quiet, and say she knew what happened but could not find words that matched it. What she did manage came in pieces.

She had been deployed in a combat setting many years ago. The parts she returns to most abruptly are sensory and positional rather than orderly: the chopping sound of helicopters overhead, the pressure of command around her, the felt certainty that other people held power over where she moved and whether she was safe. In one fragment she is being directed sharply by someone above her in rank, with no room to question or slow down; in another there is aircraft noise so loud it seems to fill her chest; in another she is aware of herself moving because she is told to move, not because she has chosen it. When she tries to place these moments into a single sequence, the story slips. She says the whole thing feels so extreme that it is hard to believe it actually happened to her, as if she is describing scenes from someone else’s life and then being shocked to remember they are hers.

In the years after returning home, the memory did not stay in the past in any settled way. It came to mind suddenly, without warning, in the middle of ordinary tasks. A helicopter passing overhead could stop her in place before she even consciously knew why. The sound would pull up those disconnected pieces so quickly that for a moment the present thinned out. She also found herself reacting strongly in situations that involved hierarchy or control. Meetings with forceful administrators or clients at work were especially difficult if someone spoke in a way that suggested they had total authority and expected immediate compliance. As a curriculum designer, she is often in conference rooms with school leaders and district staff, and she has developed a habit of choosing a chair nearest the door before anyone else sits down. She tells herself it is practical, but she knows she is scanning exits the moment she enters.

Over time, her world became smaller. She began avoiding going out unless she had to. She ordered what she could online, turned down invitations, and preferred workdays that allowed her to remain at home with her materials rather than travel to schools or district offices. Even when she did go out, she arranged herself carefully in space, staying near an exit in cafés, workshops, and waiting rooms. The habit has shaped her relationships as much as her routines. Friends from earlier parts of her life gradually stopped asking her to join them when she so often declined. Mereana feels this as a painful separateness. She looks at other people moving easily through the world and feels set apart from them, as if they share some ordinary trust she does not have.

She is also careful not to let herself feel too much. Strong emotion of any kind—fear, grief, anger, even excitement—seems risky to her, something that could break open those pieces she struggles to contain. So she flattens things when she can, changes the subject in her own mind, and keeps herself focused on tasks. Yet this control has left her unsure of herself. She has come to doubt whether she can trust herself to do the right thing when pressure rises. In work settings, if a conflict escalates or a senior person becomes directive, she can feel a familiar uncertainty take over: she must stay alert, must keep watch, must not relax. She describes living as though she has to be on guard all the time.

What finally brought her to seek help was a recent incident during an in-person curriculum meeting downtown. A helicopter passed low overhead while a district official was pressing the group for immediate changes. Mereana felt the memory surge up in jagged pieces, and although she stayed in the room, she could barely follow what was being said. Afterward she sat in her car for a long time, shaken by how quickly she had lost her footing. She told herself she could not keep organizing her life around doorways, weather, and who might take command of a room. Still, what frightens her most about treatment is being asked to say plainly what happened when words have always failed her. What she hopes, quietly, is not to become someone else, but to be able to remain in the life she has without feeling that any aircraft sound or any powerful voice can abruptly take it away.
